_voice_note: gemini-3.1-flash-tts-preview. NO speed parameter: OpenAI's speed time-stretches the audio and that artifact is what sounded synthetic. Timings are packed against measured audio; each line declares only the gap that follows it.
_direction_note: Gemini's direction must stay SHORT and plainly instructional — a longer characterful brief trips a non-configurable PROHIBITED_CONTENT block on benign lines (0/3 vs 3/3 measured). Energy level L2 on pipeline/energy-ladder.mjs: L1 was judged too hot, L3/L4 too flat. Voice Alnilam; Charon is the sanctioned alternative.
direction: Speak clearly at a natural pace, with quiet confidence and a little warmth.
direction_openai: Confident and warm, never hyped and never flat. Push gently through each line; no dramatic pauses. Read commands and file paths crisply.

explainer._purpose: The flagship 16:9 explainer: open on the viewer's own last session (the expensive model renaming a variable), turn on the manager who deploys a routed team, then pay every claim off on the live board — where the aside you mutter mid-run becomes ticket T-9 — and close on the retro that writes what it learned into your repo.

lines.text: Your most expensive model just renamed a variable. In the same chat, it judged an authentication boundary.
One chat, one model, every job. That is why the bill is high, and the work gets worse.
You didn't install a tool — you hired a manager. He runs the team; you only talk to him.
He interviews you first — batches of at most four, each with his recommendation.
Then he stops asking. The plan becomes tickets, on a board.
Then the team goes out. A scout reads the repo. Cheap tier, read only.

Implementers take one story each, on their own branch, with an empty scrollback. What they find goes into the journal in your repo — so the reviewer starts already knowing it, and a crash or a compaction changes nothing.
The reviewer grades the diff and cannot edit it. Otherwise it approves its own patch.
A good manager doesn't put a principal engineer on a grep. Roles resolve to tiers, in one file.
Security review always gets the strongest tier — and no flag or cost setting can lower it.
All of it lands on one page. Five agents running. Two questions waiting on you.
That card crossed into done by itself. Nobody dragged it there. This is Tyran, building Tyran.
Halfway through, you remember something else. So you say it.
It doesn't land in the scrollback. It becomes a ticket. Queued as T nine.
A real decision comes back with a recommendation, not a shrug. You answer here, and the run carries on.
Then the bill. Four and a half million tokens, across four hundred and four requests.
Fifty-five percent of those tokens were the manager's own context. The manager gets its own row, so nothing hides inside the total.
The scout's whole reconnaissance cost three cents. This is not an estimate. It is the bill.
None of this is a prompt asking nicely. A hook decides before the tool ever runs.
A commit carrying a secret is refused. Even inside a markdown file.
A report with no command output is refused too. It blocks silence, not forgery.
You try to close the session. It refuses. Once. The team runs the retrospective on itself.
One lesson is promoted. One is rejected. One is retired. Work you keep asking for becomes a skill.
The same failure three times becomes knowledge. Five times, it becomes a rule in your repo.
That was one request. You made two decisions. The team did the rest.
Two commands inside Claude Code, then slash tyran setup. It's open source.

onboarding._purpose: The teach-cut for someone who has just decided to try Tyran and wants to be productive today: install it, set it up on a real repository, run something real, read the board, answer a question from the board, and understand what the retro did afterwards. Eight drawn chapters, every command on screen exactly as it is typed, the manager metaphor kept alive but never sold. Every figure on screen exists in this repo or in the captures; no savings percentage, no model name, no promise the docs do not make.

lines.text: This is the whole first session. Install it, set it up on a real repo, run something, read the board.
One idea to hold on to. Tyran is a manager for a team of agents. You stay the stakeholder.
Install is two slash commands inside Claude Code. Then restart. Hooks and agents load at session start.
Slash tyran hello is the smoke test. If it answers, you are running. The only requirement is Claude Code two point one.
Slash tyran setup, once per repository. It reads how the repo is really worked. Not how the docs describe it.
Every value it infers carries the fact that produced it. And it never grants itself the right to merge to main.
Then commit the dot tyran folder. Agents work in git worktrees, and a worktree carries no untracked files.
Type slash tyran and describe the work. He interviews you first. At most four questions.
After you accept the plan, the questions stop. Shall I continue is forbidden in the conductor's own file.
Then the team goes out. A scout reads the repo first. Cheap tier, read only, fresh context.
Implementers take one story each, on their own branch. Every one starts with an empty scrollback.
The reviewer has no editing tools at all. A reviewer who can fix what they found approves their own patch.
Open the board. One command, and this is the one place a Node version matters.
Overview answers one question. Is anything on fire. Two waiting on you. Five agents running. Forty-seven percent merged.
The Board tab is every ticket, in exactly one of ten lanes. Moving a ticket means appending an event.
Say something halfway through and it does not land in the scrollback. It becomes a ticket. Queued as T nine.
The queue carries its open count in the tab label. A question you cannot see is a question you do not answer.
Each card says whether a default is recorded. Type your answer. Press Answer. And the run carries on.
Spend is what it cost. By model, by agent type, by ticket. The scout's whole reconnaissance was three cents.
Fifty-five percent of those tokens were the manager's own context. Its own row, so nothing hides. Tyran does not know what you pay. You write the rate card.
Two hooks will refuse things. A report with no command output is one. It blocks silence, not forgery.
And a commit carrying a secret is refused. Even inside a markdown file. Install gitleaks first, or that gate has nothing to scan with.
When the last ticket merges, try to end the session. It refuses. Once.
It reads the journals and the reports, then changes Tyran itself. Never your product code. Most retros change nothing, and that is correct.
The same failure three times becomes knowledge, pasted into every matching handoff. Five times, it becomes a rule in your CLAUDE file.
One line in a STOP file halts everything, from anywhere. You keep every decision. The team does the rest.

board._title: The Board — your agents move their own tickets
board._purpose: The board-first short. It opens ON a live kanban that is already moving and never leaves it: ten lanes, a blocker that says how long it has stood still, a spoken aside that hardens into ticket T-9 with a journal receipt, a card an agent crosses into DONE by itself, a real question answered on the page with the tab count ticking 2 to 1, and the bill broken out by role until the scout's three cents does the arguing. It ends on the sandbox — click it yourself, nothing to install — because the board is the only proof the delegation story needs and the sandbox is that board, already published.

retro._purpose: The 9:16 short for the self-improvement loop — the pillar no competitor has. It makes the retro visible as a mechanism rather than a promise: the Stop gate that refuses one turn, the retro reading the record (never your mood), a shallow question edited out of the conductor's own instructions, three repeated requests hardening into a skill that must earn its context, a knowledge entry retired on its own counters, a candidate rejected by a named filter, and the 3-to-knowledge / 5-to-law ladder ending in a CLAUDE.md fence carrying the five dated entries that earned it. The spine is arithmetic the viewer can audit: the knowledge panel opens at 5 entries, drops to 4, climbs back to 5, and lands exactly where it began. That is "the more you use it, the better it gets" proved as restraint rather than accumulation. One destination: the sandbox board.
